title: Negotiation & Bargaining
question: When two parties need each other but want different things, what determines whether they reach an agreement, how much value it creates, and who captures that value?

overview.text: Executives negotiate far more often than their calendars show. Budgets, hires, vendor contracts, partnerships, the division of scarce staff between departments, the terms on which a colleague will support your proposal: each is a negotiation, whether or not anyone calls it one. This week treats negotiation as a discipline with an analytic core, a body of behavioral evidence and an ethical boundary, rather than as a talent some people are born with.

The five lessons build in sequence. Lesson 1 sets out the architecture every negotiation shares: alternatives, reservation values, aspirations and the zone of possible agreement. Lesson 2 shows how value is created from differences between the parties, through logrolling and contingent contracts, and why the moves that create value expose you to the moves that claim it. Lesson 3 brings in the psychology: anchoring and first offers, the fixed-pie perception, fairness, emotion and the evidence on gender, read carefully. Lesson 4 moves negotiation inside organizations and across borders: agents and principals, internal mandates, coalitions and culture. Lesson 5 draws the line between hard bargaining and deception and distinguishes statements from commitments.

The evidence this week is mixed in kind, and you should keep track of which kind you are reading. Some of the most influential ideas, including BATNA and principled negotiation, are practitioner prescriptions. Others rest on laboratory experiments with simulated negotiations, meta-analyses of many such studies, or surveys of stated judgments. Each lesson says which is which and where the evidence runs out.

You will practice in the Negotiation Chamber, a four-issue licensing negotiation against a rule-based counterpart; analyze an international financial-services case in which the hardest negotiations happen inside each organization; and write a negotiation strategy memo for a hypothetical negotiation you could plausibly lead. The week also prepares you for the cumulative midterm that follows it, which asks for a negotiation plan alongside behavioral and evidentiary analysis.

objectives: Prepare a negotiation by estimating both sides’ BATNAs, reservation values and aspirations and the resulting zone of possible agreement.
Identify distributive, integrative and compatible issues and construct trades and contingent terms that move an agreement toward the Pareto frontier.
Apply the evidence on anchoring, fixed-pie perception, fairness and situational moderators to decisions about first offers and defenses, stating that evidence’s limits.
Design mandates, incentives and processes for negotiations conducted through agents, with internal constituencies, among several parties or across cultures.
Distinguish legitimate competitive tactics from deception, including paltering, and distinguish estimates from commitments.
Write a negotiation strategy memo that a decision-maker could approve and a negotiator could execute.

lessons.title: The Architecture of a Negotiation: Alternatives, Reservation Values and the Zone of Agreement
lessons.summary: Before anyone speaks at the table, each side’s alternative, reservation value, aspiration and opening determine whether a deal is possible and roughly where it can land.
objectives: Define BATNA, reservation value, aspiration and ZOPA, and derive a reservation value from an uncertain alternative.
Determine whether a zone of possible agreement exists from both sides’ reservation values, and explain what should happen when it does not.
Explain how alternatives, deadlines, commitments and information asymmetry shape bargaining power.
lessons.executive: Most negotiations are decided before the meeting. Your best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA) is what you will do if talks fail; your reservation value converts it into the worst terms you should accept; your aspiration sets how much of the available surplus you try to claim. The other side carries the same numbers, hidden from you. A deal is possible only when reservation values overlap (the ZOPA), and where it lands inside that zone depends on information, anchors and perceived power. The executive discipline: estimate both sides’ numbers explicitly, improve your alternative before you negotiate, and never let the table talk you below what walking away is worth.

explore.text: Consider two senior data engineers interviewing for the same role at a payments company. They are equally skilled and equally articulate. One holds a written offer from another firm that expires on Friday; the other has only a current job she is eager to leave. The company makes both the same initial offer. Almost everyone can say instantly which candidate is in the stronger position. Far fewer can say precisely what that strength consists of, how large it is, or what the second candidate should do about it. This lesson supplies that precision. (Hypothetical example.)

Now change industries. A mid-sized city is renegotiating its waste-collection contract, and the incumbent hauler asks for a 22 percent increase. The city’s position depends far less on its negotiator’s charm than on a question its public-works director should have answered months earlier: could the city run collection itself, or bid the work to a second hauler, and at what cost? If the answer is known and credible, the hauler’s demand meets a ceiling. If nobody has done the work, the city is negotiating with nothing behind it, and the hauler can usually tell. (Hypothetical example.)

Before reading on: for a negotiation you expect to face in the next six months, write down what you will do if no agreement is reached. Then write down what the other side will do if no agreement is reached. Which answer are you less sure of, and what would it cost to find out?

understand.text: Four numbers on each side

Roger Fisher and William Ury’s *Getting to Yes* introduced the term [BATNA](#gl:g-batna), the best alternative to a negotiated agreement, and argued that it, rather than an arbitrary “bottom line”, is the standard against which any proposed agreement should be measured. A BATNA is a course of action, not a number: accept the other firm’s offer, bring waste collection in-house, license to the second customer, keep the old system. Developing it starts with listing what you could actually do if no agreement is reached, then improving the most promising options and choosing the best of them.

The analytic tradition associated with Howard Raiffa’s *The Art and Science of Negotiation* converts that course of action into a number. Your [reservation value](#gl:g-reservation-value) is the point at which you are indifferent between agreeing and taking your BATNA. Your counterpart has one too. When the most a buyer would pay exceeds the least a seller would accept, every price between the two leaves both better off than walking away. That overlap is the [zone of possible agreement](#gl:g-zopa) (ZOPA). When reservation values do not overlap, no agreement is better for both than their alternatives, and the correct outcome is a polite impasse.

Two further numbers complete the structure. Your [aspiration](#gl:g-aspiration), or target, is the outcome you are realistically trying to achieve; it sits well above your reservation value and governs how much of the zone you try to claim. Your opening offer is the first number you put on the table; it sits at or beyond your aspiration so that you have room to concede. The reservation value protects you from bad deals. The aspiration protects you from mediocre ones. Negotiators who prepare only a reservation value tend to settle near it, because it is the only number they have thought hard about.

understand.text: Information asymmetry and bargaining power

Each side knows its own reservation value and must estimate the other’s. That [information asymmetry](#gl:g-information-asymmetry) drives distributive bargaining: each party tries to learn the other’s reservation value while concealing its own, and tries to persuade the other that its own is less flexible than it really is. Most tactics you will meet are attempts to move those estimates: “this is the board’s limit”, “we have another bidder”, the long silence after an offer, the deadline that appears late in the process.

Bargaining power, in this frame, is not a personality trait. It is primarily the relative cost of no deal. The side whose alternative is closer to the value of the agreement needs the agreement less and can credibly claim more of the zone. Deadlines matter because they change alternatives over time: the engineer’s outside offer expires Friday; a licensee’s regulatory audit approaches. Commitments matter because a credible statement that you cannot accept less, such as a board resolution or a published price schedule, moves the other side’s estimate of your reservation value. Reputation matters because in repeated relationships, how you claim value today changes which alternatives you will have tomorrow.

understand.title: Prerequisite: turning an uncertain alternative into a number

blocks.text: Alternatives are often uncertain. If the competing offer might be withdrawn, you can approximate its value with a probability-weighted average, called an expected value. Suppose the outside offer is worth $180,000 a year if it holds, which you judge 70 percent likely, and you fall back on your current salary of $150,000 if it does not. The expected value is 0.7 × 180,000 + 0.3 × 150,000 = 126,000 + 45,000 = $171,000. (Hypothetical numbers.)

Expected value is a starting point for judgment, not a replacement for it. A person who dislikes risk might set a reservation value somewhat below $171,000; a person who badly wants to leave the current job might set it above, because staying has costs the salary figure omits. What matters is that the adjustment is deliberate and written down before the conversation, not improvised under pressure.

understand.title: Methodological note: prescriptive analysis and descriptive research

blocks.text: Raiffa’s book is often described as a bridge between popular negotiation advice and formal game theory. It moves from two parties bargaining over one issue, to two parties with many issues, to negotiations among many parties, and uses cases such as the Panama Canal and Camp David negotiations to illustrate the analysis.

This course uses that analysis prescriptively: it tells one negotiator how to reason, given realistic assumptions about how the other side behaves. That differs from classical game theory, which assumes every party reasons flawlessly, and from behavioral research, which documents how real negotiators depart from the analysis. The two views complement each other. The prescriptive frame tells you what to calculate; the behavioral evidence in [Lesson 3](#w07-l3) tells you where your calculations, and your counterpart’s, are likely to be distorted.

challenge.text: The BATNA–reservation value–ZOPA structure is the most useful single preparation tool in negotiation. It is also a simplification, in at least four ways that matter for executives.

items: **Alternatives are rarely one number.** A competing job offer differs in location, title, team and risk; a second vendor differs in quality and switching cost. Collapsing an alternative into a figure requires judgments about what you value, and those judgments are where self-deception enters. Negotiators who want a deal tend to undervalue their alternatives.

**Reservation values should move, but for reasons.** New information during the negotiation, such as what the other system really does or how long implementation will take, should change your reservation value. Fatigue, sunk effort and a pleasant counterpart should not.

**Power is not only alternatives.** Deadlines, commitments, coalitions, legal rules, public scrutiny and the future of the relationship all affect outcomes. A city with a strong alternative may still settle generously because a service gap would be politically intolerable.
**The model is single-issue at heart.** Real deals have several issues. Treating a five-issue negotiation as one price hides the trades that create value, the subject of [Lesson 2](#w07-l2).

challenge.text: *Getting to Yes* deserves the same scrutiny you would give any influential framework. It is practitioner prescription drawn from its authors’ experience, not a report of controlled studies. Its principles (separate the people from the problem, focus on interests rather than positions, invent options for mutual gain, insist on objective criteria) have proven durable in teaching, and later laboratory work on joint gains is broadly consistent with them. But the book says less about the distributive moment when someone must give up money, and a negotiator who treats it as a complete theory can be outmaneuvered by one who claims hard. Read it as a vocabulary and a set of heuristics.

Your knowledge of the structure also has a psychological payoff. In Galinsky and Mussweiler’s experiments, the advantage of making the first offer disappeared when the recipient concentrated on the offerer’s alternatives, the offerer’s reservation price, or the recipient’s own target. Knowing the architecture is therefore not only an analytic aid; it is a defense against being pulled by the other side’s numbers.

challenge.title: Executive twist: you have not priced your alternative, and the offer expires at noon

blocks.text: You lead a department that has negotiated for three months with an analytics vendor. At 7 p.m. the vendor’s chief revenue officer calls: sign by noon tomorrow at a price 15 percent above your budget, or the price rises and the implementation slot goes to another client. You have never formally priced your alternative. A reasonable twelve-hour plan:

items: Separate the deadline from the decision. Ask what makes the deadline real and whose interest it serves; exploding offers are a common claiming tactic.
Build a rough BATNA in hours rather than weeks: call the second-ranked vendor, and estimate what a six-month delay would cost in staff time and lost capability.
Write a provisional reservation value before the call, with the reasoning behind it.
If you still cannot estimate a reservation value, treat that ignorance as information. Accepting an exploding offer is sensible only when the cost of delay clearly exceeds the premium being demanded.

apply.text: Worked example from healthcare. A regional hospital system is negotiating a two-year contract with a nurse staffing agency for intensive-care coverage. The hospital’s BATNA is to accelerate permanent hiring and pay overtime in the meantime; its finance team estimates an all-in equivalent of $112 an hour once vacancy risk is included, so the hospital’s reservation value is $112. The agency’s BATNA is to place the same nurses with another health system; after its own costs, it would accept as little as $98 an hour from this hospital. The ZOPA is $98 to $112, a $14 surplus per hour. The agency opens at $125. (Synthetic numbers.)

Three lessons follow. First, the agency’s opening sits outside the zone, which is normal; it tells you about the agency’s strategy, not about its reservation value. Second, the hospital’s strongest response is not a counter-number pulled from the air but a counter-offer near its aspiration (say $103) justified by objective criteria such as published regional rates, together with a credible signal of its alternative: “We have approved twenty permanent positions and start interviews next month.” Third, the hospital should know in advance what would change its reservation value. Learning that the agency guarantees continuity of the same nurses for the full term, which reduces training costs, is a legitimate reason to pay more. Learning that the agency is impatient is not a reason to pay less than fair value if the relationship will be renewed.

The same structure governs negotiations in player development, most of which are not about player contracts. When you negotiate a license for a biomechanics or tracking system, a lease for a training facility abroad, a data-sharing arrangement with a university laboratory, or your department’s budget with your own leadership, the questions are identical: what will you do if this does not happen, what is that worth, and what is the other side’s equivalent? An internal budget request has a BATNA too: reallocating from another line, phasing the project, or running a smaller pilot. You are stronger in the meeting when you have priced that alternative beforehand, and more credible when you can say what you will do if the answer is no.

items: Write your BATNA as an action, then as a number, with the assumptions behind the number.
Estimate the other side’s BATNA with a range and a confidence level, and list what you would need to learn to narrow it.
Set your reservation value and aspiration in writing before the first conversation.
Identify one way to improve your BATNA before you negotiate, and one way the other side might be improving theirs.
Decide which commitments, deadlines or criteria you will use to make your claims credible.

The ZOPA tells you whether a deal is possible; information, credibility and aspiration decide where in the zone it lands. Bargaining power is mostly the relative cost of no deal, which you can often change before the meeting.

takeaways: Your BATNA is a course of action; your reservation value is that action translated into the worst acceptable terms here.
A deal is possible only when reservation values overlap; when they do not, impasse is the correct outcome.
Aspirations, not reservation values, determine how much of the zone you claim; prepare both in writing.
Bargaining power is mainly the relative cost of no deal, shaped by alternatives, deadlines, commitments and reputation.
Knowing the structure is also a psychological defense against the other side’s anchors.

check.prompt: A seller will accept no less than $3.4M for a business unit (its reservation value). A buyer will pay at most $4.1M (its reservation value). The seller opens at $4.6M and the buyer at $3.0M. How wide is the zone of possible agreement, in millions of dollars?
check.working: The ZOPA runs from the seller’s reservation value ($3.4M) to the buyer’s reservation value ($4.1M): 4.1 − 3.4 = $0.7M. Opening offers do not define the zone; they are claims about it.
check.explanation: The zone is bounded by reservation values, not by opening offers: $4.1M − $3.4M = $0.7M. The openings ($4.6M and $3.0M) sit outside the zone, which is normal, and the gap between them ($1.6M) overstates the real bargaining range.

lessons.title: Creating and Claiming Value: Integrative Bargaining, Logrolling and Contingent Contracts
lessons.summary: Valuable deals are built from differences in priorities, forecasts, risk tolerance and timing, but the moves that create value also expose you to the moves that claim it.
objectives: Distinguish distributive, integrative and compatible issues and identify the sources of joint value in a multi-issue deal.
Construct a logrolling trade and a contingent contract, and judge an agreement against the Pareto frontier.
Explain the negotiator’s dilemma and choose information-sharing moves that create value without giving it away.
lessons.executive: Negotiators who split the difference on every issue routinely leave a large share of the available value unclaimed by anyone. Value comes from differences: one side cares more about price, the other about speed; one expects strong results, the other doubts them; one can bear a risk more cheaply. Trading across issues (logrolling) and making terms depend on future facts (contingent contracts) turn those differences into gains for both. The obstacles are perceptual, because negotiators assume the pie is fixed, and strategic, because revealing your priorities helps create value and helps the other side claim it. Executives need both skills: enlarge the pie deliberately, then divide it firmly.

explore.text: A cloud-services provider and a mid-sized bank spend six weeks negotiating a three-year hosting agreement. They are $400,000 a year apart on the fee, and each negotiator has told colleagues that the other side is difficult. In the seventh week a junior lawyer for the bank asks why the provider keeps resisting the bank’s request to store all data in-country. The answer surprises everyone: the provider already runs an in-country data center with spare capacity and had assumed the bank wanted a costly bespoke arrangement. The bank, for its part, cares far more about data residency, which its supervisors scrutinize, than about the fee. Within a day the parties agree on in-country hosting, a slightly higher fee and the longer term the provider wanted for its own financing. Both report a better deal than they expected. Nothing about either side’s interests changed in week seven. What changed was what each knew about the other’s priorities. (Hypothetical example.)

Before reading on: when two negotiators split the difference on each of four issues, what share of the available joint value do you guess they leave unclaimed? Write a number. You will test the guess in this week’s Negotiation Chamber.

understand.text: Two activities in one conversation

David Lax and James Sebenius describe every negotiation as two intertwined activities. Creating value enlarges what is available to divide, through sharing information about priorities, inventing options and solving problems jointly. Claiming value determines who gets what, through withholding sensitive information, anchoring and committing to favorable terms. Their central claim is that the two are inextricably linked. Earlier advice tended to address one or the other; managers face both in the same conversation.

An issue is [distributive](#gl:g-distributive-bargaining) when one side’s gain is the other’s loss, point for point: the fee in a license, the price of a building. Bargaining is [integrative](#gl:g-integrative-bargaining) when the parties can find agreements that leave both better off than other agreements they could reach, usually because they value the issues differently. Most real negotiations are mixed. Some issues are distributive, some integrative, and a few are compatible: both sides want the same outcome, such as confidentiality or an early start, without realizing it.

understand.text: Raiffa’s analysis treats two-party, multi-issue bargaining as a different problem from single-issue haggling. With one issue, every gain for one side is a loss for the other. With several issues that the parties value differently, they can trade across issues and improve both positions.

Keep trading until no package can make one side better off without making the other worse off, and you have reached the [Pareto frontier](#gl:g-pareto-frontier). An agreement below the frontier is inefficient: some other package would be better for at least one party and worse for neither. Inefficiency is not a moral failing. It is money, time or capability that neither side receives.

understand.text: Notice two things. The logroll leaves both parties better off than the split (40 against 30 each), so it is not a compromise but an improvement. And “winning” every issue produces no more joint value than splitting: the hospital captured everything, but the pie did not grow. Price, the only purely distributive issue, was held at the middle in both of the first two packages; the gains came entirely from speed and length.

understand.text: Why do capable negotiators miss trades like these? Leigh Thompson and Reid Hastie reported that most negotiators enter a negotiation expecting the other side’s interests to be completely opposed to their own, and argued that misperceiving the other side’s interests is a primary cause of inefficient agreements. This [fixed-pie perception](#gl:g-fixed-pie) leads negotiators to treat every issue as distributive and to split differences issue by issue.

A related mistake is assuming that on every issue the other side wants the opposite of what you want. On compatible issues, both want the same thing; a negotiator who “concedes” such an issue, or demands payment for it, wastes value or credibility.
Contingent contracts: betting on disagreement

When parties disagree about the future, the disagreement itself can create value. A founder convinced that her company will reach $40 million in revenue next year and a buyer who doubts it can argue about price indefinitely. Or they can agree on a base price plus an earnout that pays more if revenue reaches the target. Each side is then paid according to its own forecast, and both may prefer the contingent deal to any fixed price. Performance bonuses, success fees, price-adjustment clauses and options to extend are all [contingent contracts](#gl:g-contingent-contract). They work only under conditions:

items: The trigger is observable to both sides and measurable without dispute.
The party that controls the outcome cannot easily manipulate the measure.
The contingency does not distort behavior in ways that destroy value elsewhere, such as a revenue target that rewards discounting.
The terms are enforceable and specify who measures, when, and how disputes are resolved.

understand.title: Prerequisite: Pareto efficiency in plain language

blocks.text: An outcome is Pareto efficient when no change could make someone better off without making someone else worse off. Imagine plotting every possible agreement on a chart, your points on one axis and the other side’s on the other. The outer edge of that cloud is the frontier. Points inside it are wasteful, because moving outward helps someone and hurts no one. Efficiency says nothing about fairness: an agreement that gives one side almost everything can sit on the frontier. Negotiators therefore face two separate questions: are we on the frontier, and where on it are we?

understand.title: Methodological note: how researchers measure joint gains

blocks.text: Laboratory studies of integrative bargaining usually give each negotiator a confidential point schedule, as this week’s Negotiation Chamber does, and measure the sum of both sides’ points against the maximum available. The design makes efficiency measurable and comparable across pairs. Its cost is realism: the experimenter, not the negotiators, assigns values; issues are separable; and there is no future relationship.

Studies with managers rather than students, and with coded transcripts rather than outcomes alone, strengthen the inference. Wendi Adair, Tetsushi Okumura and Jeanne Brett coded what U.S. and Japanese managers actually said in an integrative simulation and linked patterns of information exchange to the joint gains pairs achieved, a design you will meet again in [Lesson 4](#w07-l4).

challenge.text: “Win–win” is one of the most abused phrases in management. Three cautions keep the idea honest.

items: **Integrative potential is an empirical question.** Some negotiations are genuinely distributive: one issue, one-shot, no relationship. Pretending otherwise invites concessions labelled “creative” that are simply concessions.

**Creating value says nothing about who gets it.** In the logrolling example, a sharper licensor could have taken most of the gain by also holding the price high. A deal can be efficient and lopsided at once.

**Joint gains can come at third parties’ expense.** Two department heads who trade support for each other’s budgets may both “win” while the organization loses; two firms that logroll may be colluding against customers. Efficiency between the parties at the table is not efficiency for everyone affected.

challenge.text: The [negotiator’s dilemma](#gl:g-negotiators-dilemma) is the sharpest form of the problem. If you reveal that implementation speed matters enormously to you, a cooperative counterpart will trade for it efficiently, while an opportunistic one will concede speed slowly and charge heavily for it. If you conceal your priorities, you protect yourself but make the efficient trade harder to find. Because creating and claiming are linked, neither pure openness nor pure secrecy is safe.

Experienced negotiators manage the dilemma with moves that are practitioner heuristics rather than tested rules. Share relative priorities (“speed matters more to us than term”) before anything resembling a reservation value. Reciprocate disclosure in small steps and notice whether the other side does the same. Put two or three complete packages of equal value to you on the table at once, often called multiple equivalent simultaneous offers, and learn from which one the other side prefers. Ask diagnostic questions (“What would a longer term let you do?”) rather than leading with positions.

The fixed-pie finding should itself be read with care. The error is assuming opposition without checking, not believing in opposition. In a genuinely distributive negotiation the negotiator with a fixed-pie view is simply correct, and later work in this literature makes exactly that point. The skill is diagnosis: test for differences before you conclude there are none.

apply.text: Worked example from finance and law. A private-equity buyer and the founder of a pharmacy-software company are $12 million apart: the founder values the company at $90 million on her growth forecast; the buyer will pay $78 million on its own. A contingent structure might offer $78 million at closing plus up to $12 million if audited recurring revenue in the second year exceeds an agreed target. The founder is paid on her forecast if it proves right; the buyer pays more only when the business is worth more. The drafting questions decide whether the earnout creates value or a lawsuit: who controls pricing and sales hiring after closing, how revenue is defined, whether acquisitions count, and how disputes are resolved. [Week 11](#w11) returns to these clauses. (Synthetic numbers.)

Player development is full of integrative structure. In a technology agreement, a club typically cares more about data access, integration with its own systems and support during the busiest weeks of the season than about a modest difference in fee; the vendor cares about a multi-year commitment, a reference customer and permission to describe the partnership. When two departments share scarce staff, such as a biomechanist or a video coordinator, they usually differ in when they need the person, which is an ideal setting for a trade across time rather than a contest over headcount.

Decide in advance what you will disclose about relative priorities, and what you will not disclose about your reservation value.

lessons.title: The Psychology of Bargaining: Anchors, Fairness, Emotion and Context
lessons.summary: Real negotiators are pulled by first numbers, misread the other side’s interests, reject offers they see as unfair even at a cost, and perform differently depending on the situation — patterns you can anticipate and design around.
objectives: Decide when to make the first offer and how to defend against an anchor, using the experimental evidence and its limits.
Explain why fairness norms constrain agreements, using meta-analytic ultimatum-game evidence.
Interpret the meta-analytic evidence on gender and negotiation outcomes without over- or under-claiming, and name the organizational levers it suggests.
lessons.executive: Negotiation outcomes are shaped by predictable psychology. First offers anchor settlements, so an informed first offer is usually an advantage, and the best defense against the other side’s anchor is to reason from your own preparation rather than from their number. Counterparts reject offers they see as unfair even when accepting would beat their alternative, so fairness is a second floor beneath every deal. Outcomes also depend on the situation: a large meta-analysis finds that gender differences in negotiated results shrink or reverse with experience, clear information about the range, and advocacy for others. The executive implications are practical: prepare numbers in writing, justify claims with criteria, and design processes that remove ambiguity.

explore.text: A hiring manager at a consulting firm asks a candidate for a senior data-science role: “What are your salary expectations?” The candidate has researched the market, but the range she found is wide. If she names a number first, she may set the anchor around which the conversation revolves, or she may name a figure below what the firm had budgeted and never learn it. If she declines, the firm’s first number becomes the anchor. Which risk is larger, and does the answer depend on what she knows? (Hypothetical example.)
Before reading on: in a negotiation where neither side knows much about the market value, does making the first offer help or hurt the person who makes it? Commit to an answer and one reason.

understand.text: First offers as anchors

Adam Galinsky and Thomas Mussweiler ran three experiments on simulated price negotiations. Whichever party made the first offer, buyer or seller, obtained the better outcome, and first offers strongly predicted final settlement prices, both face-to-face and over e-mail. A first offer works as an [anchor](#gl:g-anchoring): a starting point from which later judgments adjust, usually insufficiently.

The same experiments tested defenses. The first-offer advantage disappeared when the recipient focused on information inconsistent with the offer: the offerer’s alternatives, the offerer’s reservation price, or the recipient’s own target. The practical translation is direct. When the other side opens, do not reason from their number. Reason from your preparation, say so, and put your own number and its justification on the table.

understand.caption: A first-offer decision rule (practitioner heuristic built on the evidence above)

steps.label: Assess information
steps.text: Do you have reliable data on the zone: comparables, market rates, the other side’s alternatives?

steps.label: Informed: open
steps.text: Open first, ambitiously but defensibly, near or beyond your aspiration, with criteria attached.

steps.label: Uninformed: listen
steps.text: Invite their offer or ask questions first; an uninformed opening can give away surplus.

steps.label: Re-anchor
steps.text: Whoever opened, restate your analysis and counter promptly with your own justified number.

blocks.text: In judgment research, an anchor is a number that is present when you make an estimate and pulls the estimate toward itself, even when you know the number is arbitrary or self-serving. People start from the anchor and adjust, but the adjustment usually stops too early. In negotiation the anchor is rarely arbitrary; it is a deliberate claim by someone who benefits from your adjusting too little. The defense is not to ignore the number, which rarely works, but to bring a competing reference point of your own: your target, the other side’s alternative, or an objective criterion.

understand.text: The fixed pie in the mind

Recall from [Lesson 2](#w07-l2) that most negotiators enter talks expecting the other side’s interests to be completely opposed to their own. Thompson and Hastie argued that such misperceptions are a primary cause of inefficient agreements. The psychology matters beyond missed trades: a negotiator who assumes opposition tends to discount the other side’s concessions (“if they offered it, it cannot be worth much”) and to read requests on compatible issues as hostile.
Fairness as a second floor

In the ultimatum game, one player, the proposer, divides a sum of money. The other, the responder, either accepts, and both are paid as proposed, or rejects, and both get nothing. A purely self-interested responder should accept any positive amount, so a purely self-interested proposer should offer the smallest possible amount.

People do not play that way. Hessel Oosterbeek, Randolph Sloof and Gijs van de Kuilen pooled 75 results from 37 published papers. Proposers offered on average about 40 percent of the pie. Responders’ behavior varied across regions, and rejection rates fell when the pie was larger and when the share offered was larger. Responders reject offers they regard as unfair even though rejection costs them money.

For negotiators, the implication is that the other side’s reservation value is not the only floor. A counterpart who regards your offer as insulting may reject a deal that beats its alternative, especially when it can punish you at modest cost to itself. Fairness norms, built from precedent, comparable deals and the history of the relationship, act as a second constraint beneath every agreement. Objective criteria help precisely because they convert a claim into a standard the other side can accept without appearing to lose.
Emotion at the table

This lesson does not present a specific study on displayed emotion; treat what follows as practitioner heuristics to test against your own experience. Emotion carries information: visible frustration signals that you are near your limit, and visible relief after a concession signals that you would have paid more. Emotion is also contagious and can escalate a negotiation beyond its stakes. A workable discipline is to name your own state before an important session, decide in advance which reactions you are willing to show, and treat the other side’s displays as data to interpret rather than as instructions to follow.
Who negotiates, and in what situation

A meta-analysis by Jens Mazei and colleagues pooled 51 studies with 10,888 participants from several countries to compare the economic outcomes women and men obtain in negotiations. The difference favoring men was not fixed. Women did better when negotiating on behalf of another person, when they had information about the bargaining range, and when they had negotiation experience. The pattern points to situations, more than stable traits, as the source of much of the gap, and the authors emphasize that the difference can be lessened or even reversed.

understand.caption: Reading the gender evidence: what it supports and what it does not
rows: The difference depends strongly on context and shrinks or reverses in some conditions
Ambiguity about what is negotiable can widen gaps
Information about the bargaining range was one of the moderators
The role of advocate changes outcomes
Yes, on average across these studies
Negotiating for another person was associated with better outcomes for women
A lab effect size predicts the pay gap in your organization
Mostly simulated negotiations; effects do not transfer one-for-one to field settings

understand.title: Methodological note: what meta-analytic moderators can and cannot tell you

blocks.text: A moderator analysis in a meta-analysis compares the average effect across groups of studies, for example studies in which participants negotiated for themselves versus for someone else. It is powerful because it pools thousands of participants. It is also correlational at the level of studies: the studies that used advocacy roles may differ from the others in samples, tasks, years or countries, and any of those differences could account for part of the moderator effect. Treat moderators as strong leads about levers worth testing in your own setting, not as proven causal switches.

The ultimatum-game meta-analysis illustrates a second limit: the outcome is behavior in a stylized one-shot game, mostly with students and modest stakes. The robust lesson, that offers perceived as unfair are rejected at a cost, travels well. The specific percentages do not transfer to a multi-issue contract.

challenge.text: The first-offer advantage is real in the laboratory, but executives who apply it mechanically make four predictable mistakes.

items: **It assumes the offer is informed.** An opening made without knowledge of the zone can be too generous, and then the anchor works against you: the other side accepts quickly and you never learn what they would have paid.

**Extreme anchors carry costs the studies did not test.** An offer the other side sees as absurd may end the conversation or damage a relationship you need, which is exactly what the fairness evidence predicts.
**Most evidence comes from single-issue price simulations.** In multi-issue deals, repeated relationships and markets with transparent prices, a single number has less room to work.

**Robust effect, uncertain magnitude.** Anchoring in general has held up well in judgment research; the size of first-offer effects in high-stakes field negotiations, and the reliability of specific countermeasures, are less well established.

challenge.text: The gender evidence demands the opposite discipline: resisting two tempting simplifications. One reads any average difference as a fixed trait of individuals. The other dismisses the evidence because effects vary. The meta-analysis supports neither. It shows a context-dependent pattern with plausible organizational levers, measured mostly in simulations, with gender recorded as a binary category and outcomes measured in economic terms only. That is enough to justify changing processes you control; it is not enough to predict how any particular person will negotiate.

Fairness evidence has its own limits. Responders in the ultimatum game cannot make counteroffers, cannot walk away to an alternative and usually face a stranger once. Real counterparts can do all three. The constraint survives the translation; the specific numbers do not.

apply.text: Worked example from government procurement. A state agency buying a case-management system receives the vendor’s first proposal: $14 million. The agency’s estimate, built from three comparable implementations, is $9–10 million. Following the evidence, the agency’s team does not respond to $14 million by proposing $12 million. It presents its own estimate and the comparables, names its alternative (extending the current system with a smaller contractor), and asks the vendor to explain the difference line by line. The conversation now revolves around two reference points, one of them the agency’s. (Hypothetical example.)

In player development, anchors appear in staff hiring (the first salary figure mentioned), in vendor pricing and in internal budget requests, where last year’s number anchors this year’s. A practical response to the gender evidence is to reduce ambiguity in your own staff processes: share ranges where policy allows, tell every candidate explicitly what is negotiable, and use the same structured conversation for each person. These moves are consistent with the moderators in the meta-analysis and with ordinary fairness, and they require no assumptions about any individual.

items: Before the meeting, write your target, your reservation value and your estimate of the other side’s reservation value.
If you are well informed, open first, near or beyond your target, with the criteria that justify it.
If they open, acknowledge the offer without bargaining from it; restate your analysis and counter with your own justified number.
Concede in decreasing steps and explain each one; unexplained concessions invite further pressure.
Watch for signs that the other side feels treated unfairly; when you see them, return to criteria and precedent rather than to pressure.

retain.text: Informed first offers anchor outcomes, and anchors are best resisted by reasoning from your own preparation. Fairness is a second floor beneath every deal: counterparts reject insulting offers even at a cost. Outcomes depend on the situation as well as the person, which gives executives process levers rather than stereotypes.
Name the three kinds of information that eliminated the first-offer advantage in Galinsky and Mussweiler’s experiments.
Explain why a deal that beats the other side’s BATNA can still be rejected.
State one claim about gender and negotiation that the meta-analysis supports and one that it does not.

takeaways: Informed first offers tend to anchor settlements; uninformed ones can give away surplus.
Defend against an anchor by focusing on the other side’s alternatives, their reservation price or your own target.
Offers perceived as unfair are rejected even at a cost; objective criteria make claims acceptable.
Gender differences in negotiated outcomes are context-dependent; reducing ambiguity is an organizational lever.
Most of this evidence is from simulations: robust in direction, uncertain in field magnitude.

check.prompt: A supplier opens a negotiation with a price 40 percent above your estimate of fair value. You have done thorough preparation. What is the best immediate response, based on this lesson’s evidence?

options.text: Counter at the midpoint between their price and your estimate, to show good faith.
Set their number aside, restate your own analysis (including their likely alternatives) and counter with your own justified figure.
Ask them to justify their number and make no counteroffer for the rest of the meeting.
Accept a small discount immediately to avoid an impasse.

check.explanation: Galinsky and Mussweiler found that the first-offer advantage disappeared when recipients focused on information inconsistent with the offer, such as the offerer’s alternatives and reservation price or their own target. Re-anchoring with your own justified number brings a second reference point into the conversation.

optionFeedback.a: A midpoint counter lets their anchor define the range; you would be splitting a difference they chose.
optionFeedback.c: Asking for justification is useful, but leaving their number as the only figure on the table lets the anchor work for the rest of the meeting.
optionFeedback.d: Conceding immediately rewards the anchor and signals that your preparation does not bind you.

check.prompt: What is the main flaw in this reasoning?

stimulus.text: “A meta-analysis of 51 studies found that men obtain better economic outcomes in negotiations on average. So when we choose who negotiates our vendor contracts, we should assign men.” (Hypothetical argument.)

options.text: Meta-analyses cannot be used for organizational decisions.

It treats a context-dependent average as a fixed individual trait; the same evidence shows the difference shrinks or reverses with experience, information about the range and advocacy for others — conditions that apply to a trained professional negotiating for the organization.
The sample of 51 studies is too small to show anything.
The argument is flawed only because it might be illegal; the reasoning itself is sound.

check.explanation: The meta-analysis shows strong situational moderation. A professional negotiating on behalf of an organization, with experience and information about the range, is in exactly the conditions under which the difference was smaller or reversed. Averages across simulations also say little about any individual.

optionFeedback.a: Meta-analyses are among the best evidence available; the error is in how this one is read.
optionFeedback.c: Fifty-one studies with more than ten thousand participants is a substantial evidence base.
optionFeedback.d: Legal concerns are real, but the reasoning is also statistically and logically wrong, which is the flaw asked about.

lessons.title: Negotiating Through Others and Across Borders: Agents, Constituencies, Coalitions and Culture
lessons.summary: Executive negotiations are usually conducted by agents, must be ratified by people who are not at the table, often involve more than two parties and frequently cross cultural lines — each of which changes the analysis.
objectives: Diagnose principal–agent problems in a negotiation and design mandates and incentives that reduce them.
Plan an internal negotiation that builds a mandate and anticipates ratification before the external negotiation begins.
Use cross-cultural evidence on information exchange to adapt your approach while avoiding national stereotypes.
lessons.executive: In organizations, the person at the table is rarely the person who bears the outcome. Agents, whether executives, brokers, lawyers or your own staff, bring expertise and distance, but their incentives and information differ from their principals’. Every external deal also needs internal approval, and the constituencies that must ratify it can be a liability or a source of credible commitment. With three or more parties, coalitions form and sequence matters. Across cultures, negotiators exchange information differently; evidence shows mismatched routines lower joint gains, while cultural labels explain less than stereotypes suggest. Align mandates and incentives before the first meeting, and adapt to the counterpart you observe, not to a nationality.

explore.text: A hospital network’s chief procurement officer negotiates for four months with a medical-device maker and reaches a five-year agreement she considers excellent: a 9 percent price reduction, guaranteed supply and training for nursing staff. At the board’s finance committee, the agreement stalls. The cardiology department objects that the contract standardizes on a device its surgeons consider inferior; the chief financial officer asks why the term is five years when a competing product is expected within eighteen months. Told of the delay, the device maker withdraws the training commitment. The external negotiation was skilled. The internal one never happened. (Hypothetical example.)
Before reading on: list everyone who would have to approve, implement or live with the outcome of a negotiation you expect to face this year. Which of them have you not yet consulted, and why not?

understand.text: Agents and principals

A [principal–agent problem](#gl:g-principal-agent) arises when one party, the agent, acts for another, the principal, whose interests or information differ. Negotiation is full of them: the sales executive paid on signed bookings rather than profitability; the broker paid a percentage of price, who gains little from holding out for a slightly better deal; the department head negotiating a vendor contract her successor will live with; the adviser whose fees grow with the length of a dispute. Agents also bring real benefits: expertise, market knowledge, emotional distance and a built-in reason to pause (“I need to take this back to my client”).

understand.caption: Agents in negotiation: benefits, risks and controls
rows: The agent knows more than the principal, who cannot judge the deal
Require the agent’s reasoning, comparables and alternatives in writing
Incentives diverge: pay for volume, speed or hours rather than outcome
Review and align incentives before granting the mandate
The agent overcommits, or the counterpart goes around the agent
A written mandate: what the agent may agree and what needs approval
Relationships with the other side’s agent
Agents close deals that serve their careers or their relationship

understand.text: Agency changes behavior as well as incentives. In the meta-analysis by Mazei and colleagues, women obtained better economic outcomes when they negotiated on behalf of another person than when they negotiated for themselves. Acting as an advocate can license an assertiveness that self-advocacy does not, one reason organizations often assign negotiations to someone other than the person who benefits.
The internal negotiation and ratification

Every external deal is also an internal one. Before you negotiate with a vendor, partner or other organization, you negotiate a mandate with the people whose support you need: the budget holder, the unit that will implement, legal and compliance, and those whose work will change. Think of it as negotiating at two levels at once. What you can agree at the external table is bounded by what your constituencies will ratify, and what they will ratify depends on what you can credibly bring back.

understand.caption: Two-level preparation: the internal negotiation comes first

steps.label: Map constituencies
steps.text: Who must approve, who will implement, who can veto or quietly undermine?

steps.label: Negotiate the mandate
steps.text: Agree interests, reservation value, authority limits and acceptable trades in writing.

steps.label: Negotiate externally
steps.text: Stay within the mandate; report signals back early, especially bad news.

steps.label: Ratify
steps.text: Bring a package and its reasoning, not a surprise.

steps.label: Implement
steps.text: The people who live with the deal decide whether its value is realized.

understand.text: Ratification constraints cut both ways. A narrow mandate makes you predictable and slows the deal. But a genuine constraint (“our board will not approve a term beyond three years”) can move the other side’s estimate of your reservation value, as [Lesson 1](#w07-l1) described. The constraint helps only if it is real. A manufactured constraint is a form of deception, and when it is discovered it damages every later claim you make.
More than two parties

Raiffa’s analysis treats negotiations among many parties as a distinct problem from two-party bargaining. Once three or more parties are involved, subsets can agree among themselves and present terms to the rest, so the question is not only what each party gets but who is inside the agreement.

items: Map who needs whom: a party’s leverage depends on which coalitions it could join or block.
Sequence deliberately: early commitments from respected parties make later ones easier, while a visible early refusal can unravel a coalition.
Identify blocking coalitions: parties that cannot build an agreement can often stop one.
Keep side arrangements transparent enough to survive discovery by the other members.

understand.text: Across cultures

Wendi Adair, Tetsushi Okumura and Jeanne Brett studied Japanese and U.S. managers negotiating an integrative simulation with partners from their own culture and from the other. U.S. negotiators shared information directly, asking and answering questions about priorities, and avoided influence tactics, within and across cultures. Japanese negotiators exchanged information more indirectly and used influence with each other, but adapted their behavior with U.S. partners. Intercultural pairs reached lower joint gains than same-culture pairs, and culturally typical behaviors partly explained the gap.

The mechanism is more useful than the national profiles. When two negotiators use different routines for discovering priorities, one asking direct questions and the other inferring priorities from the pattern of offers, each may conclude that the other is evasive or naive, and the trades that depend on shared information go unfound. The remedy is to make the routine explicit: say how you would like to exchange information, and notice how your counterpart prefers to.

How much does national culture explain? On one side, studies such as Adair, Okumura and Brett’s find systematic differences in negotiation behavior between national groups, with consequences for joint gains. On the other, the ultimatum-game meta-analysis by Oosterbeek and colleagues found that regional differences in responder behavior were, with one exception, not explained by standard cultural classifications such as Hofstede’s and Inglehart’s. Both can hold at once: behavior differs on average across groups, yet the indices used to label cultures predict it poorly, and variation within any country is large.

understand.title: Prerequisite: what “culture” means in this research

blocks.text: In negotiation research, culture usually means the shared norms, values and practices of a group, and in most studies it is measured by nationality. That is a convenient proxy, not a definition. Nationality bundles language, legal institutions, industry norms and personal history, and any difference attributed to “culture” could come from any of them. When you read that negotiators from one country behave differently from those of another, read it as a statement about averages in a particular sample and task.

The ecological fallacy is the inference from a group average to an individual member of the group. If one national sample shares information more directly on average than another, it does not follow that the person across the table from you will. Distributions overlap heavily; a single counterpart’s training, industry, age and organization may matter more than nationality. The research supports adapting to observed behavior and to explicit conversation about process. It does not support scripting your approach from a country label.

A second caution concerns coverage. The evidence cited in this lesson compares the United States with Japan, and the ultimatum-game meta-analysis pools regions coarsely. Neither directly studies negotiations between U.S. and Dominican or other Caribbean parties. Applying these findings there is reasoned inference, which is useful, but it is not evidence about that setting.

challenge.text: Three tensions resist tidy solutions. First, aligning an agent’s incentives with the principal’s is harder than it sounds: pay an agent on closing and the agent becomes eager to close; pay only on long-run outcomes and the agent becomes overcautious. Every compensation formula creates its own distortion, a problem [Week 8](#w08) treats in depth.

Second, building an internal mandate takes time, and time can weaken your external position: a counterpart may lose interest, or a deadline may pass. Some executives respond by negotiating externally first and seeking forgiveness later. That sometimes works, but it spends credibility you will need for the next deal, and it exposes the agreement to the kind of collapse described in the hospital example.

Third, adaptation across cultures has limits. Adapting your information-exchange style to a counterpart is evidence-based; imitating what you believe to be their culture can read as condescension, and in many international settings your counterpart is also adapting to you. The most robust move is meta-communication: talking explicitly about how you will negotiate, how decisions get approved on each side, and how you will confirm understandings.

challenge.title: Executive twist: you are the agent, and your mandate is ambiguous

blocks.text: Your organization’s president asks you to “get the partnership with the overseas training facility done this month, but don’t overpay.” You ask for a number; the answer is “use your judgment.” You will be judged on both the deal and its cost, by someone who has not said what either means.

items: Write the mandate you think you have: target, reservation value, the trades you may make and the issues you may not concede. Send it to the president for a one-line confirmation before you negotiate.
Name the constituencies you will consult (finance, legal, compliance, the staff who will use the facility) and what each must see.
Agree on what counts as “overpaying” in terms of an alternative: what would you do if this facility were unavailable, and what would that cost?
Plan how you will tell the counterpart, truthfully, which terms you can agree and which require approval.

apply.text: Worked example from government and the military. Three allied governments negotiate cost-sharing for a joint training facility, with a prime contractor as a fourth party. Each delegation needs its legislature’s approval. Two governments quietly agree on a cost formula and present it to the third as nearly settled, a coalition move that speeds agreement but risks resentment. The third delegation’s strongest response is not to fight the formula but to use its ratification constraint: it cannot win legislative approval without a share of the contractor’s local work, a term the contractor values little because it already has a local supplier. The constraint is real, it creates value, and it is disclosed openly. (Hypothetical example.)

International operations in professional baseball combine every element of this lesson. A partnership for an academy in the Dominican Republic or elsewhere in Latin America may involve a landowner, a facility operator, community stakeholders, your own leadership and compliance staff, and intermediaries who act as agents for one or more parties. Fluency in English and Spanish is a real asset, but language is not the same as shared negotiating routines: within any country, urban and rural, corporate and family-run, older and younger counterparts differ. Observe how a particular counterpart exchanges information, say plainly how you would like to exchange priorities (“It would help us to know which of these issues matters most to you; for us it is the training schedule”), know who on each side must approve, and confirm understandings in writing in both languages.

items: Write the mandate and get it confirmed by the person whose authority you are using.
List every agent involved, on both sides, and how each is paid.
Map the parties beyond the table and decide the order in which you will consult or approach them.
Plan the information-exchange process explicitly, especially across languages or organizational cultures.
Decide what you will report back, when, and to whom, before you sign anything.

retain.text: The person at the table is often an agent whose incentives and information differ from the principal’s, so mandates and incentives must be designed before negotiation begins. Internal ratification bounds external agreement and, if real, can strengthen it. Across cultures, mismatched information-exchange routines cost joint value; adapt to the counterpart you observe rather than to a country label.
Give two examples of principal–agent conflict in a negotiation you know, and one control for each.
Explain how a genuine ratification constraint can improve your bargaining position, and why a manufactured one is dangerous.
What did intercultural pairs in Adair, Okumura and Brett’s study achieve, relative to same-culture pairs, and what partly explained it?

takeaways: Agents bring expertise and distance but carry their own incentives; write mandates and align pay before negotiating.
Every external deal is an internal negotiation first; ratification limits what you can agree and, when real, adds credibility.
With three or more parties, coalitions and sequencing shape outcomes as much as offers do.
Mismatched information-exchange routines lower joint gains across cultures; make the process explicit.
National labels predict individual behavior poorly; adapt to the counterpart you observe.

check.prompt: What is the most important principal–agent risk in this situation?

stimulus.text: A technology company hires an outside recruiting firm to negotiate the compensation of a new chief data officer. The firm’s fee is 25 percent of the executive’s first-year cash compensation, payable on acceptance. (Hypothetical.)

options.text: The recruiter has an incentive to close quickly at a higher salary, because its fee rises with pay and is paid only if the candidate accepts.
The recruiter will negotiate too hard and lose the candidate.
The company knows more about the market than the recruiter.
There is no agency problem because the recruiter is a professional.

check.explanation: The fee structure rewards the recruiter for a higher salary and for any acceptance, not for the company’s best outcome. The company can respond by capping or flattening the fee, setting a written compensation mandate, and keeping direct contact with the candidate at key points.

optionFeedback.b: The incentive runs the other way: a percentage fee paid on acceptance rewards closing, not holding out.
optionFeedback.c: The usual asymmetry favors the agent, which is part of why agency problems arise.

lessons.title: Where Hard Bargaining Ends: Deception, Commitments and Difficult Conversations
lessons.summary: Negotiation rewards selective disclosure, which makes the boundary between tough bargaining and deception the most consequential line an executive draws — ethically, legally and for reputation.
objectives: Classify negotiation tactics along the spectrum from legitimate competitive bargaining to deception, including paltering.
Explain the evidence on how negotiators and their targets judge deceptive tactics and what paltering costs when discovered.
Draft a personal disclosure policy and distinguish, in general terms, nonbinding statements from binding commitments.
Plan a difficult conversation that separates the relationship from the substance.
lessons.executive: Every negotiator withholds information; the question is what else you do with it. Survey evidence on tactics shows broad agreement at the extremes, where inflated opening demands are accepted and outright lies and bribery are not, and real disagreement in between. Paltering, using true statements to create a false impression, is common and often works in the short run, but targets judge it about as harshly as lying, and it raises impasse risk and reputational damage when discovered. Some misstatements also carry legal risk. Adopt a written disclosure policy before you need one, answer hard questions without lying, and keep clear which of your statements are commitments.

explore.text: Near the end of a negotiation over a two-year analytics contract, the vendor’s account executive asks you directly: “Are you talking to anyone else?” You held one exploratory call with a competitor four months ago and have not followed up. Consider four answers. (a) “Yes, we’re in discussions with another provider.” (b) “We’ve spoken with other providers.” (c) “I’m not going to get into that.” (d) “No, you’re our only option.” Which are lies? Which are true but misleading? Which would you be comfortable seeing quoted, word for word, in an e-mail to your own leadership? (Hypothetical example.)
Before reading on: rank the four answers from most to least ethical. Then note whether your ranking would change if you knew the vendor had lied to you earlier in the negotiation.

understand.text: A spectrum, not a line

Roy Lewicki and Robert Robinson asked MBA students at two business schools (320 and 736 respondents) to rate how appropriate 18 bargaining tactics were. A factor analysis found five clusters of tactics, similar across both samples. Tough but not outright dishonest tactics, such as inflating an opening demand, were widely accepted; outright lies and bribery were widely rejected. Judgments also differed with personal characteristics: in their samples, women and older, more experienced students were more conservative, and acceptability varied by school and nationality.

understand.text: Paltering

Todd Rogers and colleagues named a tactic most codes of conduct miss. [Paltering](#gl:g-paltering) is the active use of truthful statements to create a misleading impression. It differs from lying by commission, which uses false statements, and from lying by omission, which passively withholds information. Across two pilot studies and six experiments with more than 1,750 participants, paltering helped negotiators claim value, but it also made impasse more likely and harmed the palterer’s reputation. Targets judged paltering about as unethical as making false statements; palterers and outside observers judged it more favorably, and many people preferred paltering to outright lying.

The perception gap is the executive lesson. People who palter feel more honest than the people they mislead think they are. In repeated relationships, with staff, agents, vendors and partner organizations, the target’s judgment is the one that becomes your reputation. Answer (b) in the opening scenario is a palter: literally true, chosen because it will be misunderstood.

understand.title: Prerequisite: three ways to mislead, and one way not to

items: **Lying by commission:** stating something you believe to be false (“We have a competing bid at $1.2 million”).
**Lying by omission:** passively leaving out information you know the other side would consider important, in a context where silence misleads.
**Paltering:** actively saying true things selected to create a false belief.
**Declining to answer:** openly refusing to share information (“I won’t discuss our alternatives”). This is not deception; the other side knows it has not been told.

understand.text: Commitments: what binds you

*Educational material about general legal concepts — not legal advice. Consult a qualified attorney about any specific agreement.* Statements made in negotiation differ in legal weight. In many common-law systems, opinions, estimates of value and statements about your own willingness to pay are generally treated differently from statements of material fact. A misrepresentation of a material fact that the other side relies on can expose a party to claims such as fraud or misrepresentation and can allow the other side to unwind the agreement. Whether a document binds also varies: a signed contract binds; a term sheet or letter of intent may bind in part (for example confidentiality or exclusivity clauses) or not at all, depending on its wording and the governing law; an exchange of e-mails can sometimes form a contract. Rules differ across jurisdictions, including between common-law and civil-law systems. [Week 11](#w11) develops these concepts.

understand.text: Difficult conversations

Some negotiations are less about a deal than about a conflict: a staff member who believes a promotion was promised, a partner who feels misled, a colleague whose project you are about to cancel. Fisher and Ury’s advice to separate the people from the problem is a practitioner heuristic rather than tested science, but it captures the core move: treat the relationship and the substance as two problems, each needing attention. Graduate negotiation teaching treats this territory as part of the field; MIT’s open course 15.667, for example, devotes sessions to dispute prevention, mediation and difficult people.

items: Open with process before substance: what you hope the conversation will accomplish and how you propose to proceed.
Acknowledge the other person’s account of events before offering yours; acknowledgment is not agreement.
Distinguish intent from impact: “I did not intend to mislead you, and I can see that you were misled.”
Say what you can and cannot commit to, and do not soften a “no” into an implied “later” you cannot honor.
Consider a neutral third party when the relationship itself has become the obstacle.

understand.title: Methodological note: measuring ethics by survey and by experiment

blocks.text: The two studies in this lesson use different designs, and each has a blind spot. Lewicki and Robinson measured stated judgments of hypothetical tactics. That reveals norms and disagreements but not behavior: people under pressure may use tactics they rate as inappropriate, or avoid tactics they rate as acceptable. Rogers and colleagues measured behavior and reactions in controlled negotiations, which shows consequences, but the stakes were modest, detection was engineered by the design, and legal consequences were outside the study. Together they support two cautious conclusions: norms in the middle of the spectrum are genuinely contested, and paltering’s costs are underestimated by the people who use it.

challenge.text: The evidence does not settle the philosophy, and serious people disagree. Three positions recur. The first treats bargaining as a game with known conventions: everyone understands that “this is our final offer” may not be, so bluffing about limits deceives no one who understands the game. The second holds that deception is wrong regardless of convention, because it treats the other person as a means. The third judges tactics by consequences: what they do to trust, to the relationship and to the institutions that make deals possible. Each position permits declining to answer; they part company over bluffing and paltering.

What the evidence does is undercut a common rationalization, that a tactic is acceptable because everyone does it. Acceptability judgments differ by person, experience and context, and targets judge paltering more harshly than palterers do. The counterpart across the table may draw the line where you do not, and in a repeated relationship their judgment is the one that counts.

There is also a strategic tension with [Lesson 2](#w07-l2). The negotiator’s dilemma rewards some concealment, and a policy of total transparency can be exploited. The resolution most experienced negotiators reach is to be selective about what they disclose and scrupulous about the truth of what they say: decline freely, never invent, and do not arrange true facts to build a false picture.

challenge.title: Executive twist: you discover that the other side lied

blocks.text: Two weeks before signing a facility-services contract, your team learns that the vendor’s claim of “a competing offer from another client for the same capacity” was invented. The terms are otherwise good and your alternative is weak.

items: Separate the decision from the anger: does the lie change your estimate of the vendor’s reliability in performing the contract?
Raise it directly and factually, without theatrics, and observe the response; a correction is information, and so is a denial.
If you proceed, rely less on statements and more on structure: contractual representations, performance metrics, step-in rights and shorter initial terms.
Record what happened and inform the people who will manage the relationship; the next negotiator should not have to rediscover it.

apply.text: Return to the opening scenario. Answer (d) is a lie by commission, and answer (a) is close to one, since a call four months ago is not “discussions”. Answer (b) is a palter. Answer (c) is honest and protects your position, at the cost of sounding guarded. A stronger honest answer combines refusal with substance: “We explored alternatives earlier in the year. I won’t go into detail; what will decide this is value and fit, and here is where your proposal still falls short.” It is true, it does not invite a misleading inference, and it returns the conversation to criteria.

items: I will not state anything I believe to be false.
I will not arrange true statements to create a belief I know to be false about a material matter.
I may decline to discuss my reservation value, my alternatives or internal deliberations, and I will say so openly.
I will make clear which of my statements are commitments and which are estimates or intentions.
If I learn that I have made a material misstatement, I will correct it promptly.
I will verify material claims made to me and rely on written terms for what matters most.

apply.text: In player development the repeated game is unusually small. Agents, vendors, coaches and partner organizations talk to one another, and staff move between organizations. A reputation for straight dealing compounds over years; so does the opposite. When a candidate for a coaching role asks whether the position will be funded next season and you do not know, the honest answer (“the budget is not approved; here is what I can commit to, and here is when I will know more”) costs you little now and protects a relationship that may matter for a decade.

Worked example from consulting. A consulting partner is asked by a prospective client whether the firm has done this kind of work before. The firm has done one similar project, which went poorly. “We’ve worked in this sector for years” is true and misleading. The partner who instead describes the one project, what went wrong and what the firm changed afterward may lose the engagement, but she has not created a liability that will surface in the first steering-committee meeting, and clients who stay tend to trust her later estimates. (Hypothetical example.)

retain.text: Declining to disclose is legitimate; inventing facts is not; paltering sits in between in the minds of those who use it, and with lying in the minds of those it targets. Some statements carry legal weight, and the line between estimate and commitment should be clear in every negotiation you lead. A written disclosure policy is easiest to keep when it was written before the pressure arrived.
