glossary.definition: Best alternative to a negotiated agreement: the course of action you will take if this negotiation fails. It is the benchmark for judging any proposed deal.
The worst terms you would accept in this negotiation; the point at which you are indifferent between agreeing and taking your BATNA.
The ambitious but defensible outcome you are trying to achieve; it governs how much of the zone of agreement you try to claim.
The range of outcomes that both parties prefer to their alternatives; it exists only when their reservation values overlap.
A situation in which one party knows something relevant, such as its own reservation value, that the other does not. Distributive bargaining largely consists of managing it.
Bargaining over a fixed amount of value, where one side’s gain is the other’s loss; also called value claiming.
Bargaining that finds agreements better for both parties than other available agreements, usually by exploiting differences in priorities, forecasts or capabilities; also called value creation.
Trading concessions across issues, so that each side gives ground on what matters less to it in return for what matters more.
The set of agreements that cannot be improved for one party without making the other worse off. Agreements inside it leave value unclaimed.
An agreement whose terms depend on a future, observable outcome, such as an earnout or performance fee, used when parties disagree about the future.
The tension, named by Lax and Sebenius, that the moves that create value, such as revealing priorities, also expose a negotiator to the moves that claim it.
A practitioner technique: presenting several complete packages of equal value to you at once and learning about the other side’s priorities from which one it prefers.
The assumption that the other side’s interests are directly opposed to yours on every issue, which leads negotiators to miss trades and compatible issues.
A number, often the first offer, that pulls subsequent judgments and the final settlement toward itself.
An experiment in which one player proposes a split of money and the other accepts it or rejects it, in which case both get nothing; used to study fairness.
The conflict that arises when someone acting on another’s behalf has different incentives or information from the person they represent.
Approval of a negotiated agreement by people who were not at the table, such as a board, legislature or membership; it bounds what negotiators can agree.
Using truthful statements to create a misleading impression; distinct from lying by commission and from passively omitting information.

exercise.title: Negotiation Chamber

intro.text: You represent Quorvia Systems, a fictional company that licenses a camera-based quality-inspection platform, in negotiations with Brennholt Industrial, a fictional manufacturer that wants to deploy it in 14 plants. Four issues are open: the annual fee, the contract term, rollout speed and the use of anonymized inspection images. You have six rounds. In each round you either propose a complete package or ask one question about one issue; a question reveals what a good question would uncover, and it uses the round.

Watch three things: which issues the counterpart concedes first and what that suggests about its priorities; whether your package beats your alternative and by how much; and how close your final agreement comes to the maximum joint value available, which the debrief reveals. All numbers are synthetic, and the rules the counterpart follows are listed under “Show the rules”.
Before round 1, write in your notebook: which issue you think matters most to Brennholt, your target score, your reservation score, and the score you expect to end with.

role.text: You are vice president of partnerships at Quorvia Systems (fictional). Quorvia’s software inspects welds and machined parts from cameras on the production line. Brennholt Industrial (fictional) would be your largest customer. Your points table shows what each option is worth to Quorvia, as your chief executive has set priorities; higher is better, and the maximum is 100.

What matters to you, and why. Data rights matter most: anonymized images from 14 plants would substantially improve the general model you sell to every customer. Contract term matters next: a multi-year contract improves your revenue visibility before a planned funding round. The fee matters, but your board cares more about the multi-year and data story than about a few hundred thousand dollars a year. Rollout speed matters least: a faster rollout means hiring contract implementation engineers, which costs something but is manageable.
Your alternative: a signed letter of intent from a smaller manufacturer for four plants, worth about 40 points on your scale. Any agreement below 40 points is worse than walking away.

Ground rules: propose complete packages (one option on every issue). The counterpart is rule-based; it cannot be persuaded, flattered or bluffed. The exercise tests the structure of your offers, not your rhetoric.

Read the counterpart’s concessions as information. The rule-based counterpart always concedes first on the issue that costs it least for each point it gives you, so the order of its moves reveals its priorities. Human negotiators often do the same, less consistently and sometimes deliberately misleadingly. If you noticed which issues moved first and built your next package around them, you were logrolling.

The structure of this negotiation is typical of commercial deals. One issue is purely distributive: on the fee, every option gives the two companies the same combined total, so the only question is who gets it. The other three are integrative: on each, one option is worth more to the two companies combined than any other. Splitting the difference on every issue beats both alternatives, which makes it feel like success, but it leaves roughly a quarter of the available joint value unclaimed, and there are packages that are better for both sides than the split. Lessons 1–3 explain why intelligent negotiators still choose it.

case.title: The Corridor Agreement
case.fiction: All people, organizations and data in this case are fictional, and all figures are synthetic. Real places are used for setting only; nothing in the case describes any real company, cooperative, bank or regulator.

body.text: At 6:40 on a Thursday evening in Miami, Tomás Ibarra closed the door of a small conference room at Brisamar Payments and laid three documents on the table: the federation’s counterproposal, a two-line e-mail from his chief compliance officer, and the deal timeline his chief executive wanted met within ten weeks. He had until Friday at noon to present a negotiation plan to the chief executive, and until Tuesday to be back in Santiago de los Caballeros, across the table from people who had begun, he suspected, to distrust him.

Brisamar is a seven-year-old digital remittance company. Customers in the United States send money through its app to relatives in Latin America; Brisamar earns a flat customer fee on each transfer and a spread on converting dollars into local currency. Its corridor to the Dominican Republic is growing fastest, but in the northern Cibao region its recipients collect cash at a patchwork of pharmacies and small shops. Complaints about closed locations and payout points running short of cash have doubled in a year. A partnership with the Federación Cooperativa Valle Alto, eleven savings-and-credit cooperatives with 64 branches across the region, would give recipients reliable payout points and, if both sides wished, the option of depositing money into a cooperative savings account.

The federation’s executive director, Altagracia Méndez Rosario, has led it for fourteen years. Decisions on external partnerships require eight of the eleven board votes. The three large urban cooperatives around Santiago already pay out remittances for a larger U.S. competitor under a contract with 26 months left to run, and they handle most of the region’s volume. The eight rural cooperatives in mountain and border towns have no remittance partner at all; their members receive money through informal couriers or travel to the city to collect it.

The first meeting, in March, went badly in a way nobody said aloud. Tomás’s team arrived with a twenty-slide presentation and a draft term sheet. Altagracia hosted a long lunch, spoke about the federation’s founding after a hurricane, introduced her board chair and did not discuss numbers. Tomás’s notes from that day read: “Stalling? Need to push.” Three weeks later the federation’s finance director, Ernesto Vidal, younger, educated partly in the United States and notably direct, sent a counterproposal by e-mail: $2.50 per payout, 20 percent of Brisamar’s currency spread on federation transfers, no exclusivity, Brisamar to pay all training costs, and a feature in Brisamar’s app inviting recipients to open a cooperative savings account. A local consultant Brisamar hired afterward told Tomás that the board had felt “presented to, not talked with” in March, and that the lunch had been the federation’s way of deciding whether Brisamar was a partner or a vendor.

Brisamar’s standing offer is $1.75 per payout, no share of the currency spread, exclusivity at all 64 branches for three years, training costs split evenly, and no deposit feature. The product team opposes the savings-account invitation because it fears recipients will leave the app; nobody has measured whether they would.

Inside Brisamar, the positions are firm and not aligned (Exhibit 1). The chief financial officer, Marcus Feld, has told the board that the currency spread is the company’s margin and has said, more than once, “No revenue share on FX, full stop.” The chief compliance officer, Renée Albright, sent Tomás this e-mail at 5:12 p.m.: “I will not approve payouts at any branch my team has not reviewed and trained. Neither will the bank. Do not promise dates.” Brisamar’s U.S. bank partner, which is not at the table, must approve any new network of paying agents; in past expansions its approval took between four and twelve weeks. Renée estimates that bringing the rural branches up to Brisamar’s identity-verification and transaction-monitoring standards will cost about $180,000 and take eight to fourteen weeks.

The chief executive, Nadia Fernández-Hollis, wants the agreement signed before the company’s next funding round closes in about ten weeks. “Investors want to see the corridor,” she told Tomás, “but nothing that embarrasses us with the bank.” Tomás’s own annual bonus includes a component paid on new corridor volume under agreements signed by June 30. He knows this; Nadia approved it; neither has mentioned it in connection with the federation. Tomás believes, sincerely, that moving fast is in the company’s interest.

Two pieces of information complicate everything. On a call last week, Ernesto mentioned that “others” had offered the urban cooperatives $2.40 per payout. Tomás cannot tell whether this refers to the competitor’s renewal terms, a fresh proposal, or a negotiating line. If it is real, the urban cooperatives have a strong alternative and little reason to accept exclusivity. If it is not, Ernesto has bluffed, or perhaps paltered by describing an old conversation in the present tense.

The second came at a dinner in Santiago. Speaking in Spanish, without pressure and almost in passing, Altagracia told Tomás she “could find eight votes” if the rural cooperatives saw “something they can show their members” and if the urban cooperatives were “not asked to choose.” Tomás took this to mean two things: drop exclusivity for the urban cooperatives, and give the rural ones a visible benefit, perhaps funded training, technology for their branches or a bonus tied to volume. He is not certain he understood her correctly, and he has not checked.

The economics are not trivial (Exhibit 3). At Brisamar’s projected volume of 38,000 transfers a month in the second year, the gap between its current offer and the federation’s counterproposal is worth roughly $850,000 a year in contribution. But Brisamar’s current offer is not a deal; it is a position the federation has already declined. The relevant comparison is between the agreements that could actually be ratified on both sides and Brisamar’s alternative, which is to keep its patchwork of shop-based payout points in the Cibao while trying to recruit individual cooperatives one at a time, something Altagracia has signaled the federation would regard as hostile.

Tomás sketched four approaches on the whiteboard, none of them complete. The first was to accept most of the federation’s terms in order to sign fast: around $2.30 per payout, no exclusivity, Brisamar funding the training, and the deposit invitation. Marcus would object to the cost, and Renée would object to any implied launch date. The second was to hold firm on economics but restructure exclusivity: $2.00 per payout, no share of the spread, and exclusivity only with rural cooperatives that wanted it, in exchange for Brisamar funding their training. The third was contingent: a fee that rose in tiers with volume, a bonus pool for rural cooperatives if the corridor reached agreed targets, and the deposit invitation tested in a pilot with measured effects on app retention. The fourth was to slow down: sign nothing until Renée’s review was complete and the bank had approved the network, and tell Nadia that the funding round should not set the timeline for a regulated partnership.

Each approach had a constituency against it. The first threatened the margin story Marcus had told the board. The second risked the urban cooperatives, without whom the corridor would carry less than half its projected volume. The third was elegant but complicated, and Ernesto had already said the board “does not like formulas it cannot explain to members.” The fourth was the safest and the one most likely to cost Tomás his bonus, and possibly the deal.
At 8:15 Tomás opened a blank document and typed a heading: “What we need, what they need, and what we can’t promise.” Then he deleted “can’t” and typed “shouldn’t.”

questions: Map this as at least three linked negotiations: inside Brisamar, inside the federation, and across the table. Which should Tomás work on first, and what must come out of it?
Estimate each side’s BATNA and identify the issues on which their priorities differ. Which trades or contingent terms could create value, and which issue is mainly distributive?
How should Tomás treat the $2.40 figure? Draft one question he could put to Ernesto that tests it without accusing anyone of bluffing.
Identify the principal–agent problems on both sides. What, if anything, should Nadia change before Tuesday?
What did Brisamar misread in March, and how should Tomás structure Tuesday’s meeting differently without relying on national stereotypes?

perspectives.title: Build the coalition the federation can ratify
perspectives.text: Altagracia has told Tomás how to win eight votes: do not force the urban cooperatives to choose, and give the rural ones something visible. A non-exclusive master agreement with a fee between Brisamar’s offer and the federation’s ask, Brisamar-funded training for the rural branches (paid once, as an investment, rather than shared), and voluntary exclusivity for rural cooperatives in exchange for a volume bonus can be ratified on both sides. The currency spread stays with Brisamar, which protects the margin story. The risk is overpaying if the $2.40 rumor is false; Tomás should test it before conceding on fee.

perspectives.title: Do not let the funding round set the timeline
perspectives.text: Renée and the bank, not the federation, control when the first payout can happen. A signed agreement that cannot launch for three months does little for investors, and an implied launch date that compliance then refuses would damage Brisamar with the federation and the bank at once. Tomás should tell Nadia that the deadline is self-imposed, negotiate a nonbinding letter of intent now with clear statements of what is and is not committed, and sign the definitive agreement after compliance review. The cost is time and perhaps Tomás’s bonus; the benefit is a deal that does not unravel in the first audit.

perspectives.title: Use contingent terms to resolve the forecast disagreement
perspectives.text: Much of the conflict is a disagreement about the future: Brisamar fears that a deposit invitation will cost it customers; the federation believes it will build loyalty; Brisamar projects 38,000 transfers a month and the federation may doubt it. A volume-tiered payout fee, a rural bonus pool triggered by audited corridor volume, and a measured pilot of the deposit invitation let each side be paid on its own forecast. The objection is Ernesto’s: formulas the board cannot explain will not pass. The contingent terms must be few and simple, with a one-page explanation in Spanish.

perspectives.title: Fix the agent before the negotiation
perspectives.text: Tomás’s bonus rewards volume signed by June 30, which pushes him toward speed and concessions whatever his intentions. Nadia should restructure it, for example to reward twelve-month corridor contribution and clean compliance results, and should approve a written mandate (fee range, no spread share, conditions on launch dates) before Tuesday. On the federation’s side, Ernesto’s position and Altagracia’s signals may reflect different constituencies; Tomás should learn who on the board needs what rather than treating the federation as one negotiator.

case.application: The structure transfers directly to international operations in professional baseball. An agreement for a training facility or academy abroad typically has the same three tables: inside your organization (finance, legal and compliance, baseball leadership), inside the partner (owners, local institutions, community stakeholders) and across the table, often through intermediaries whose incentives differ from those of the people they represent. The same disciplines apply: build the internal mandate first, let compliance and legal set what can be promised, distinguish cultural signals from individual ones, test claims about competing offers with questions rather than accusations, and do not let an internal deadline become the other side’s leverage.

questions.prompt: A hospital is deciding how far it can go in renegotiating a contract with its outside laboratory. Its alternative is to build an in-house laboratory, which would cost $2.4M a year if the build finishes on schedule (60 percent likely). If the build is delayed, the hospital must buy a year of spot testing at $3.1M. What is the expected annual cost of the hospital’s alternative, in millions of dollars? (Synthetic numbers; ignore risk attitudes.)
questions.working: Expected cost = 0.6 × 2.4 + 0.4 × 3.1 = 1.44 + 1.24 = $2.68M. A risk-neutral hospital should not agree to pay the laboratory more than about $2.68M a year; a risk-averse one might accept somewhat more to avoid the chance of a $3.1M year.
questions.explanation: The BATNA is uncertain, so its value is a probability-weighted average: 0.6 × $2.4M + 0.4 × $3.1M = $2.68M. That figure is the starting point for the hospital’s reservation value; risk attitudes and non-financial factors then adjust it deliberately.

questions.prompt: What is the soundest conclusion for both parties?

stimulus.text: After months of talks over the sale of a software business, the seller’s board has documented that it will not sell below $5.2M, because a strategic buyer has offered $5.2M in a binding bid. The buyer’s investment committee has documented that it cannot justify more than $4.9M on its own valuation. A mediator proposes $5.05M “to meet in the middle.” Price is the only open issue, and both sides’ figures are well grounded. (Hypothetical.)

options.text: Both should accept $5.05M, since splitting the difference is fair.

There is no zone of possible agreement on price alone; unless the parties can create value on another dimension (for example a contingent payment), impasse is the correct outcome and the seller should take the strategic bid.
The buyer should accept $5.05M because it has invested months in the deal.
The seller should accept $5.05M because a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.

questions.explanation: The seller’s reservation value ($5.2M) exceeds the buyer’s ($4.9M), so no price leaves both better off than their alternatives. A midpoint is worse for each side than walking away. Only new value, such as an earnout that bridges different forecasts, could create a zone; otherwise impasse is the right result.

optionFeedback.a: Splitting the difference is not fair or sensible when it leaves both parties below their alternatives.
optionFeedback.c: Months of effort are sunk costs; they do not change what the business is worth to the buyer.
optionFeedback.d: The seller has a binding $5.2M bid in hand; $5.05M is a worse bird.

questions.prompt: Rank the four packages from highest to lowest joint value (sum of both parties’ points).

stimulus.caption: Point schedules for a facilities-management contract (synthetic)

options.text: Medium price, 4-hour response, 3-year term
Medium price, 24-hour response, 1-year term
Low price, 4-hour response, 1-year term
High price, 24-hour response, 3-year term

questions.explanation: Joint values: (a) client 10 + 30 + 0 = 40, contractor 10 + 0 + 20 = 30, joint 70; (c) client 20 + 30 + 5 = 55, contractor 0, joint 55; (d) client 0, contractor 20 + 10 + 20 = 50, joint 50; (b) client 10 + 0 + 5 = 15, contractor 10 + 10 + 0 = 20, joint 35. The logroll in (a) gives the client fast response (worth 30 to it, costing the contractor 10) and the contractor a long term (worth 20 to it, costing the client 5). Price is purely distributive: every price option adds 20 joint points, so it cannot change the ranking.

questions.prompt: A buyer and a founder agree to bridge a valuation gap with an earnout. Which trigger is most likely to create value rather than a dispute?

options.text: Post-closing EBITDA as reported by the buyer, which will control costs and allocations after closing.
Gross revenue, with no constraints on discounting.
Audited recurring revenue under defined accounting rules, with pricing floors, a defined treatment of acquisitions and a named dispute-resolution process.
The founder’s own assessment of whether the targets were met.

questions.explanation: A contingent term works when the trigger is observable to both sides, measured without dispute, and hard for the party controlling the outcome to manipulate. Audited recurring revenue with defined rules, pricing floors and a dispute process meets those conditions far better than measures one side controls.

optionFeedback.a: The buyer controls costs and allocations after closing, so it could depress EBITDA and the founder would rightly fear manipulation.
optionFeedback.b: Unconstrained revenue rewards discounting that may destroy value elsewhere.
optionFeedback.d: A measure controlled by the party being paid invites the opposite manipulation.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation is best supported by this (fictional) study?

stimulus.text: Fictional abstract. “We analyzed 312 municipal contract renegotiations. When the city made the first offer, final prices averaged 6 percent lower than when the contractor made the first offer. Among renegotiations in which the city had no recent market price data, however, city first offers were associated with higher final prices than contractor first offers. Cities chose for themselves whether to open first.”

options.text: Opening first causes cities to obtain lower prices in all circumstances.

The data are consistent with first offers helping when the opener is informed and hurting when it is not, but because cities chose whether to open, the study cannot establish that opening first caused the differences.
The study shows anchoring does not occur in real negotiations.
Because the sample is 312, the effect is certainly causal.

questions.explanation: The pattern matches the laboratory logic: informed first offers anchor favorably, uninformed ones can give away surplus. But the study is observational and cities self-selected into opening first; better-prepared cities may both open first and negotiate better. It suggests a hypothesis consistent with Galinsky and Mussweiler’s experiments without proving causation in the field.

optionFeedback.a: The study itself reports the opposite pattern when cities lacked market data, and it cannot establish causation.
optionFeedback.c: A 6 percent difference associated with who opened is consistent with anchoring, not evidence against it.
optionFeedback.d: Sample size reduces noise; it does not remove selection bias.

questions.prompt: What is the main flaw in the vice president’s reasoning?

stimulus.text: A vice president preparing a final offer to a small supplier says: “Their alternative is worth about $400,000 a year to them. Our offer is $410,000, so they will accept. Whether they think it’s fair after last year’s price cuts is irrelevant; they’re rational.” (Hypothetical.)

options.text: The vice president has overestimated the supplier’s alternative.

It assumes a counterpart accepts anything that beats its alternative; evidence from ultimatum-game research shows people reject offers they see as unfair even at a cost to themselves, so fairness is a second constraint.
Offers should always be made in round numbers.
The reasoning is sound; fairness matters only in laboratory games.

questions.explanation: Meta-analytic ultimatum-game evidence shows that responders reject offers they regard as unfair even though rejecting costs them money. A supplier that feels squeezed after last year’s cuts may refuse a deal that beats its alternative by a small margin, or accept and look for the exit. Objective criteria and attention to precedent reduce that risk.

optionFeedback.a: The estimate may be wrong, but the flaw in the reasoning holds even if the estimate is right.
optionFeedback.c: Irrelevant to the logic of the argument.
optionFeedback.d: The laboratory games simplify, but the fairness constraint they reveal is one of the more robust lessons for real deals.

questions.prompt: A company uses an outside broker, paid 3 percent of the purchase price on closing, to negotiate the purchase of a warehouse. Which measures reduce the principal–agent problem? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pay the broker a fee that increases as the purchase price falls below an agreed benchmark.
Give the broker a written mandate with a maximum price and the terms that require the company’s approval.
Let the broker decide the maximum price, since the broker knows the market better.
Require the broker to provide comparable transactions and the seller’s likely alternatives in writing before the final offer.
Keep the 3 percent fee and add a bonus for closing within two weeks.
Arrange a direct principal-to-principal conversation before the final terms are agreed.

questions.explanation: A percentage-of-price fee paid on closing rewards a higher price and any closing. Aligning pay with the buyer’s outcome, setting a written mandate, requiring the agent’s evidence and keeping direct principal contact at key moments all reduce the problem. Delegating the reservation value to the agent or rewarding speed makes it worse.

optionFeedback.c: Delegating the reservation value to the agent hands the decision to the party with the misaligned incentive.
optionFeedback.e: A speed bonus adds a second incentive to close regardless of price.

questions.prompt: What is the best next move?

stimulus.text: In a negotiation with a family-owned distributor abroad, you have asked direct questions about priorities in two meetings and received polite, general answers. Your counterpart has, however, made offers that consistently hold firm on payment terms and move readily on delivery schedules. A colleague says, “They’re evasive. That’s how people from that country negotiate.” (Hypothetical.)

options.text: Push harder with direct questions until you get a straight answer.
Accept your colleague’s cultural explanation and lower your expectations for joint gains.
Treat the pattern of offers as information about priorities (payment terms appear to matter more), propose packages that trade on it, and say explicitly how you would like to exchange information.
Switch to a single-issue price negotiation to avoid confusion.

questions.explanation: Research on U.S. and Japanese managers found that negotiators differ in how they exchange information, directly through questions or indirectly through offers, and that mismatched routines lower joint gains. Reading the offers, testing the inference with packages, and making the process explicit adapts to the counterpart you observe, without a stereotype.

optionFeedback.a: Repeating a routine that is not working is unlikely to surface priorities and may read as disrespect.
optionFeedback.b: A country label predicts an individual’s behavior poorly (the ecological fallacy), and the offers already carry usable information.
optionFeedback.d: Collapsing to one issue destroys the trades the offers are revealing.

questions.prompt: Read the negotiation notes. Select every genuine ethical or legal-commercial issue they raise.

stimulus.text: Notes from a services negotiation (fictional). (1) Our lead declined to disclose our budget when asked. (2) She told the vendor we had a “signed competing quote at $310,000”; no such quote exists. (3) The vendor said its platform “passed its last security audit”; we later learned a newer audit found open findings. (4) We opened at a price well below our target. (5) We both signed a “letter of intent” that includes an exclusivity clause for 90 days but says the letter is “non-binding”. (6) The outside adviser who introduced the vendor receives a referral fee from the vendor that we were not told about.

options.text: Item 1: declining to disclose the budget
Item 2: the invented competing quote
Item 3: the vendor’s statement about its security audit
Item 4: the low opening offer
Item 5: the letter of intent’s exclusivity clause
Item 6: the adviser’s undisclosed referral fee

questions.explanation: The invented quote is a false statement of fact and may carry legal exposure in many jurisdictions. The audit statement is a palter on a material fact. A “non-binding” letter that contains an exclusivity clause needs review, because some clauses in such letters can bind depending on wording and governing law. The adviser’s undisclosed fee is a conflict of interest, a principal–agent problem. Declining to disclose and an ambitious opening are widely accepted competitive tactics. (Educational material, not legal advice.)

optionFeedback.a: Declining to disclose is open and widely accepted; it is not deception.
optionFeedback.d: An ambitious opening is traditional competitive bargaining, widely judged acceptable.

questions.prompt: In general terms, which statement made by a seller in a negotiation is most likely to create legal exposure if it is false?

options.text: “This is the best platform on the market.”
“We won’t go below $900,000.”
“Our system is certified under the security standard your regulator requires.”
“I think you’ll find our team easy to work with.”

questions.explanation: A specific, verifiable claim about a material fact the buyer is likely to rely on is the kind of statement that can support claims such as misrepresentation. Opinions, sales talk and statements about one’s own limits are generally treated differently in many common-law systems, though rules vary by jurisdiction. (Educational material about general legal concepts, not legal advice.)

optionFeedback.a: Broad superlatives are usually treated as opinion or sales talk rather than verifiable fact.
optionFeedback.b: Statements about your own willingness to pay or accept are generally treated as negotiating positions, though they can still be ethically questionable when false.
optionFeedback.d: An expression of opinion about the future relationship is not a statement of material fact.

questions.prompt: You are negotiating a two-year contract for a video-analysis platform. Near the end of the second meeting, the vendor asks: “What’s your budget for this?” Write the response you would give (60–120 words). Then explain in two or three sentences how your response handles the negotiator’s dilemma and the ethics of disclosure.
questions.modelAnswer: Response: “I’m not going to share a budget figure; it would only anchor both of us. What I can tell you is what matters most to us: integration with our existing systems and on-site support in the first three months matter more than the license fee, and a two-year term works for us. If you can show us a package that is strong on integration and support, we can talk about how the fee fits, using what comparable organizations pay.” Explanation: The answer declines openly rather than inventing a number or paltering, so nothing in it is false or misleading. It protects the reservation value while disclosing relative priorities, which creates room for trades, and it moves the price discussion toward objective criteria.

rubric.criterion: Honesty: no false statement and no misleading true statement about budget or alternatives
levels: 0 — states or implies a false budget or alternative
1 — no false statement, but the wording invites a misleading inference
2 — declines openly; everything said is true and not misleading

rubric.criterion: Protects the reservation value while creating value
levels: 0 — reveals the budget or reservation value
1 — protects the number but offers nothing that would help find trades
2 — protects the number and discloses relative priorities or invites package proposals

rubric.criterion: Moves the discussion toward criteria or interests
levels: 1 — redirects to interests, comparables or objective criteria

rubric.criterion: Explanation links the response to the negotiator’s dilemma and disclosure ethics
levels: 1 — explains which information is shared, which is withheld, and why

questions.prompt: You will negotiate a three-year analytics partnership with a university laboratory. Your finance chief wants the lowest cost, your coaching staff want rapid access to findings, and your legal team insists on data-protection terms the laboratory has resisted before. The first external meeting is in two weeks. What should you do first?

options.text: Open talks with the laboratory immediately to learn its position, then report back to the three internal groups.
Convene the three internal groups to agree a written mandate: priorities, reservation value, non-negotiable terms and the trades you may make, then negotiate externally.
Ask the legal team to negotiate, since data protection is the hardest issue.
Let each internal group contact the laboratory directly so that each can represent its own interests.

questions.explanation: Every external deal is also an internal negotiation. Agreeing the mandate first prevents the deal from collapsing at ratification, gives you credible constraints (the data-protection terms are real) and lets you plan trades across issues the internal groups value differently.

optionFeedback.a: Learning early has value, but negotiating without a mandate risks commitments your constituencies will not ratify.
optionFeedback.c: Delegating to one function hands the whole negotiation to the group with one priority.
optionFeedback.d: Multiple uncoordinated channels let the counterpart play your constituencies against each other.

reserve.prompt: A negotiator prepares only a reservation value and no aspiration. What is the most likely consequence?

options.text: She will reach impasse more often.
She will tend to settle close to her reservation value, because it is the only number she has thought hard about.
She will anchor the other side more effectively.
Nothing; the reservation value contains all the information she needs.

reserve.explanation: The reservation value protects against bad deals but does not tell you how much of the zone to claim. Without a prepared aspiration, negotiators tend to treat the reservation value as the goal and settle near it.

optionFeedback.a: A reservation value alone does not make impasse more likely; it makes mediocre deals more likely.
optionFeedback.c: Anchoring requires an ambitious opening tied to an aspiration; the reservation value should not be revealed.
optionFeedback.d: The reservation value marks the floor, not the target.

reserve.prompt: Using the hospital–licensor point schedules from Lesson 2 (speed worth 0/15/30 to the hospital and 10/5/0 to the licensor; length of 1/2/3 years worth 0/15/30 to the licensor and 10/5/0 to the hospital; price high/middle/low worth 20/10/0 to the licensor and 0/10/20 to the hospital), how many joint points does splitting the difference on every issue leave below the maximum joint value?
reserve.working: Split (medium, 2 years, middle): hospital 15 + 5 + 10 = 30; licensor 5 + 15 + 10 = 30; joint 60. Maximum: fast speed (30 + 0 = 30 joint), 3 years (0 + 30 = 30 joint), any price (20 joint) = 80. Gap = 80 − 60 = 20.
reserve.explanation: Price always contributes 20 joint points, so the gains come from speed and length. Choosing fast rollout and a 3-year term yields 80 joint points; splitting yields 60. The 20-point gap is value neither side receives.

reserve.prompt: What is the best approach for the founder?

stimulus.text: A founder is selling a niche software product to a larger firm. She has no comparable sales data and no idea what the buyer’s internal valuation is. The buyer’s corporate-development head asks her to “name a number.” (Hypothetical.)

options.text: Name a high number immediately, since first offers always win.
Avoid naming a number until she has more information: ask questions about the buyer’s plans and alternatives, seek comparables, and, if the buyer opens, re-anchor with her own justified figure.
Ask the buyer to split the difference between two numbers she has not yet chosen.
Name a low number to build goodwill.

reserve.explanation: The first-offer advantage depends on information. Uninformed, she risks anchoring below what the buyer would pay. Gathering information first, and re-anchoring with her own analysis if the buyer opens, applies the evidence and its limits.

optionFeedback.a: The laboratory advantage assumed an informed offer; an uninformed number can give away surplus or look absurd.
optionFeedback.c: This has no content and cedes the anchor.
optionFeedback.d: Goodwill bought with a low anchor is expensive and rarely reciprocated in price.

reserve.prompt: Asked whether her company has other bidders, a seller who has none says, “We’ve had a lot of interest since the announcement,” which is true only of inquiries that went nowhere. How would the targets in Rogers and colleagues’ experiments most likely judge this statement if they discovered the facts?

options.text: As acceptable, because the statement is literally true.
As about as unethical as a false statement.
As more ethical than declining to answer.
As irrelevant, because buyers expect sellers to exaggerate.

reserve.explanation: The statement is a palter: true words chosen to create a false belief. Targets in the experiments judged paltering about as unethical as making false statements, while palterers and observers judged it more favorably, a perception gap that matters for reputation.

optionFeedback.a: That is how palterers tend to see it; targets do not.
optionFeedback.c: Declining to answer is open; paltering actively misleads.
optionFeedback.d: Expectations of exaggeration attach to opinions and openings, not to misleading statements about facts such as other bidders.

assignment.title: Negotiation Strategy Memo

brief.text: Choose a negotiation you could plausibly lead in the next year and prepare it as a senior executive would: in writing, before the first conversation, for a reader who must approve your mandate. Suitable examples include licensing a technology platform for your department, a data-sharing or research partnership with a university laboratory, an agreement for a training facility abroad, a resource or budget negotiation with your own leadership, or an offer to a candidate you are hiring.

Keep it hypothetical and non-confidential. Use fictional organization names and synthetic numbers, and mark every assumption. Do not include information about real players, colleagues, contracts or club business. The aim is to practice the analysis, not to document a real negotiation.

items: Estimate both sides’ BATNAs and reservation values with ranges and confidence, not single numbers presented as facts.
List at least four issues and score your priorities; estimate the other side’s, labelled as estimates.
Identify at least one trade and, where a forecast disagreement exists, one contingent term.
Write walk-away rules you would actually follow, and a disclosure policy you would be comfortable having quoted.

brief.text: Before writing: in one sentence, what decision does your reader need to make after reading the memo?

assignment.deliverable: A 1,000–1,500-word negotiation strategy memo, organized under the template headings, for a hypothetical negotiation you could plausibly lead.

template.heading: Situation and recommendation
template.guidance: Two or three sentences: the negotiation, what you recommend as the mandate, and the decision you need from your reader.

template.heading: Interests
template.guidance: Your interests and, separately, your best understanding of the other side’s. Distinguish interests (why) from positions (what is demanded). Name internal constituencies on both sides.

template.heading: BATNA — both sides
template.guidance: Your BATNA as a course of action and its estimated value; the other side’s likely BATNA with a range and your confidence. Note how either could be improved before the negotiation.

template.heading: ZOPA estimate
template.guidance: Both reservation values (yours firm, theirs estimated), the resulting zone, your aspiration, and what would change your reservation value for good reasons.

template.heading: Issues and trades
template.guidance: At least four issues with your priority points (summing to 100) and estimated priorities for the other side. Mark each issue distributive, integrative or compatible; propose the trades and any contingent terms.

template.heading: Opening strategy
template.guidance: Whether you will open, with what package, and the criteria that justify it; how you will respond if they open first.

template.heading: Concessions plan
template.guidance: The sequence and size of concessions, what you will ask for in return for each, and which issues you will not concede.

template.heading: Information to seek
template.guidance: The questions that would most change your plan, how you will ask them, and what you will disclose about relative priorities.

template.heading: Walk-away rules
template.guidance: Explicit conditions under which you will stop, pause or escalate, including deadlines and who must approve exceptions.

template.heading: Relationship and ethics
template.guidance: Your disclosure policy for this negotiation, how you will handle being asked about your budget or alternatives, ratification steps, and what the relationship should look like after signing.

rubric.criterion: Analytic preparation: interests, both BATNAs, reservation values and the ZOPA

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Both sides’ interests, BATNAs and reservation values are estimated with ranges, explicit assumptions and confidence; the ZOPA follows logically; good reasons to revise are named.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: All elements present and reasonable; some estimates lack ranges or stated assumptions.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Own side analyzed; the other side’s BATNA or reservation value is asserted without reasoning.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Positions are listed in place of interests; BATNA or ZOPA is missing or confused with an opening offer.

rubric.criterion: Value creation: issues, priorities, trades and contingent terms

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Four or more issues with scored priorities; distributive, integrative and compatible issues identified; trades and a contingent term are specific and plausible.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Multiple issues and at least one credible trade; contingent options thin or generic.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Issues listed but treated mostly as separate price-like contests.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Single-issue framing; no trades.

rubric.criterion: Claiming strategy: opening, concessions and walk-away rules

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Opening decision justified by information and criteria; concession plan is sequenced and conditional; walk-away rules are explicit and credible.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Sound opening and concessions; walk-away rules present but partly vague.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Opening chosen without rationale; concessions unplanned or unconditional.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No opening, concession or walk-away plan.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Identifies the few unknowns that matter most, how to learn them, what to disclose and what to protect; assumptions are labelled throughout.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Useful questions and a disclosure stance; some assumptions unlabelled.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Generic questions; no disclosure plan.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Treats estimates as facts; no information plan.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: A specific disclosure policy with no deceptive or paltering tactics; internal mandate and ratification steps planned; post-agreement relationship considered.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Ethical stance and ratification addressed, with limited specificity.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Ethics mentioned generically; ratification ignored.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Plan relies on misleading statements or ignores who must approve.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Recommendation and decision needed in the first paragraph; concise, organized under the headings, within the word range.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Clear and organized; recommendation slightly buried or some redundancy.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Hard to find the recommendation; uneven sections.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No clear recommendation; disorganized.

scenario.text: Draft your negotiation strategy memo for a reader who must approve your mandate before you negotiate. Lead with the recommendation and the decision needed, then work through the template headings.

audience.who: The executive who must approve your mandate
audience.cares: What you will agree to, what it costs, what you will not concede, and what could go wrong.
Economic limits, binding commitments, data and regulatory terms, and who signs.

checklist: Recommendation and decision needed appear in the first two sentences
Both BATNAs are stated as actions with estimated values and ranges
At least one trade across issues and, where relevant, one contingent term
No statement in the plan would mislead the other side if quoted
All names and numbers are fictional or synthetic, and assumptions are labelled

prompts: Recall a negotiation from the past two years whose outcome you later regretted. Which number did you not prepare well: your BATNA, your reservation value, your aspiration, or your estimate of the other side’s? What would preparing it have changed?
Where is your default on the negotiator’s dilemma: do you tend to disclose too much or too little? Give one concrete example as evidence, and one situation in which your default served you badly.
Write the disclosure policy you actually followed in your last difficult negotiation, not the one you would like to have followed. Where do the two differ, and why?
Think of a negotiation conducted across languages or organizational cultures. What did you assume about how the other side exchanged information, and how, if at all, did you check that assumption?

review.front: What is a BATNA, and how does it differ from a reservation value?
review.back: A BATNA is the course of action you will take if talks fail; the reservation value converts it into the worst terms you would accept in this deal.
Only when the most one side would give exceeds the least the other would accept — when reservation values overlap. Otherwise impasse is the correct outcome.

review.front: Why prepare an aspiration as well as a reservation value?
review.back: Negotiators who prepare only a floor tend to settle near it; the aspiration governs how much of the zone you try to claim.

review.front: In the BATNA framework, what is bargaining power mainly?
review.back: The relative cost of no deal, shaped by alternatives, deadlines, credible commitments and reputation.

review.front: What is the difference between a distributive and an integrative issue?
review.back: Distributive: one side’s gain is the other’s loss. Integrative: the parties value it differently, so a trade can leave both better off.

review.front: Why can a logroll beat splitting the difference for both sides?
review.back: Each side gives ground on what it values less and gains on what it values more, moving the agreement toward the Pareto frontier.

review.front: What conditions does a contingent contract need?
review.back: An observable, measurable trigger that the controlling party cannot easily manipulate, no value-destroying distortions, and enforceable terms with a dispute process.
Moves that create value (sharing priorities) expose you to moves that claim it; creating and claiming cannot be separated (Lax and Sebenius).

review.front: What eliminated the first-offer advantage in Galinsky and Mussweiler’s experiments?
review.back: The recipient focusing on the offerer’s alternatives, the offerer’s reservation price, or the recipient’s own target.

review.front: What is the fixed-pie perception, and when is it not an error?
review.back: Assuming the other side’s interests are completely opposed to yours. It is correct in genuinely distributive negotiations; the error is assuming it without checking.

review.front: What does ultimatum-game evidence imply for negotiators?
review.back: People reject offers they see as unfair even at a cost, so fairness is a second floor beneath the other side’s reservation value.

review.front: What did the Mazei et al. meta-analysis find about gender and negotiation outcomes?
review.back: A difference favoring men that depended on context and shrank or reversed with advocacy for others, information about the range, and experience.

review.front: Name three controls for a principal–agent problem in negotiation.
review.back: A written mandate with authority limits, incentives aligned with the principal’s outcome, and required evidence plus principal contact at key moments.

review.front: Why did intercultural pairs reach lower joint gains in Adair, Okumura and Brett’s study?
review.back: Partly because their information-exchange routines differed (direct questions versus indirect inference from offers).

review.front: What is paltering, and how do targets judge it?
review.back: Using true statements to mislead. Targets judged it about as unethical as lying; palterers judged it more favorably.

preview.text: The midterm that follows this week asks you to combine behavioral analysis, evidence evaluation, leadership judgment and a negotiation plan in one case. After it, Week 8 turns the principal–agent problem into a question of organizational design, incentives and decision rights. Week 11 treats the commitments that negotiations produce as contracts — formation, representations and warranties, contingent terms and dispute resolution — and Week 13 returns to the ethics of disclosure as a matter of governance.

links.why: Incentives for agents and decision rights are organizational-design problems.
Negotiated terms become contract clauses; misrepresentation and binding documents are developed there.
Ethics and governance under uncertainty extend this week’s disclosure policy.
